Article Title: 'Left' in existential crisis: From CPI-CPM rift in Kerala to Delhi rout, old fault lines deepen
Article Text:
The Left faces a deeper political challenge as electoral setbacks, internal tensions and shrinking influence converge

Pinarayi probe: Another challenge after Kerala defeat

DUSU polls: Why isn't Left mobilisation becoming votes?

CPI vs CPM: When opposition itself becomes a battlefield

From Bengal to Kerala: How did the Left reach here?

What next for the Left?

There was a time when the Left’s political footprint stretched from West Bengal to Tripura and Kerala. Its influence travelled further still, through trade unions, university campuses, farmers’ movements and a cadre network that kept the red flag visible even where Communist parties were not in power. That map has steadily grown smaller.For India’s Left, the question is no longer only about shrinking electoral numbers. It is increasingly about where the Communist movement still has the political space, organisational confidence and social influence to assert itself. In Delhi, the SFI-AISA alliance has struggled to translate visible participation in student mobilisations into votes. In Kerala, the two principal constituents of the Left Democratic Front, the CPM and CPI, have found themselves publicly at odds over even the distribution of positions within the opposition, and that too after a heavy defeat in the assembly elections.These may appear to be separate battles, but they have come at a particularly difficult moment for the Left. The Kerala defeat has left it without a state government, the CPM and CPI are publicly disagreeing over the way forward, former chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan is facing a probe, and the Delhi university results have again exposed the gap between the Left’s visibility in student movements and its electoral reach.The timing makes these developments particularly significant. The Left’s retreat has been a long process. The fall of the Left Front in West Bengal in 2011, the loss of Tripura in 2018 and the steady decline in its parliamentary strength had already reduced the Communist parties’ national footprint. Kerala had remained the exception, a state where the Left retained a durable organisational network and, in 2021, even broke the state’s established cycle of alternating between the LDF and UDF governments. Its defeat in 2026 means that India currently has no state government led by a Communist party.But the more revealing question may be what is happening beneath the election results. Is the Left merely going through another electoral trough, particularly after a decade in power in Kerala, or are the latest developments exposing older fault lines, from leadership and alliance tensions to the difficulty of converting traditional political mobilisation into electoral support?On September 22, the UDF government ordered a police inquiry based on an Enforcement Directorate report concerning allegations involving former chief minister and current leader of opposition Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter Veena T and son-in-law PA Mohammed Riyas in the CMRL-Exalogic case. The state government said the inquiry would be entrusted to the state police; reports said it would initially be conducted by the Crime Branch without registration of an FIR.The underlying allegations are already part of an ED investigation. The agency has alleged financial irregularities involving payments made by Cochin Minerals and Rutile Ltd to Veena's now-defunct company Exalogic Solutions, and has sought action against Vijayan and others. The Kerala government's decision followed legal advice on whether the information and material supplied by the ED warranted a preliminary inquiry.For the CPM, however, the political dimension is inseparable from the legal one. Party general secretary MA Baby has said the party will fight the matter “legally and politically”, while accusing central agencies of having been used against opposition leaders.That places the Left in an unfamiliar position in Kerala. For a decade, Vijayan and the CPM were operating from government. Now the former chief minister is leading the opposition while facing a probe ordered by the government that replaced him.The probe comes only months after the LDF lost power following a decade in government, at a time when the CPM is already examining what went wrong and trying to regroup in opposition. The question is therefore not simply whether the allegations withstand investigation. The episode also puts Vijayan and the record of the previous government back under scrutiny at a particularly difficult moment for the party.The Delhi University Students' Union election offers a different window into the Left's problem, particularly its ability to convert activism and issue-based mobilisation into electoral support.The SFI-AISA alliance had been visible in campaigns around issues including student housing, examinations and accountability, and had participated prominently in the CJP mobilisation. Yet its electoral numbers declined in three of the four central-panel contests compared with 2025. Its presidential candidate Ananya Raturi received 5,377 votes, almost identical to the 5,385 polled by the alliance's candidate last year. But its vice-presidential tally fell from 4,163 to 2,383, the secretary vote from 9,535 to 8,734 and the joint-secretary vote from 8,425 to 5,837.The results also showed that student politics cannot simply be read as a binary contest between the major national parties and the Left. ABVP won three of the four central-panel positions, while Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen won the vice-president's post with 30,615 votes. He had previously been associated with Congress-affiliated NSUI but contested independently after not receiving its ticket.For the Left, the striking element is the gap between mobilisation and electoral conversion. A political organisation can be prominent in protests, articulate grievances on campuses and participate in wider movements, but that visibility does not automatically translate into votes.The presidential contest is particularly revealing. The Left candidate finished with 5,377 votes, while ABVP's Yash Dabas won with 24,576 and NSUI's Vijay Shankar Meena polled 22,523. The result does not erase the Left's presence on campus, but it does expose the difficulty of turning that presence into control of student institutions.And that is why the DUSU result matters beyond one university election. Student politics has historically been an important space for the Left to recruit, organise and build its next generation of political workers. Sitaram Yechury, for instance, rose through student politics at JNU before eventually becoming CPI(M) general secretary.The question for the Left now is simpler: if it can still bring young people to protests and movements, why is it struggling to bring them to the ballot box?The strain is also visible inside Kerala's Left alliance. After the LDF's assembly defeat, the CPI demanded the post of deputy leader of the opposition in the assembly, arguing for a larger role within the alliance. The CPM, however, rejected the demand, with Vijayan publicly opposing it.On the surface, the disagreement is about a post. But underneath it is a larger debate about how the LDF should function after its election defeat. The CPI has argued for greater sharing of responsibilities and “collective leadership”, while the CPM has maintained that the alliance should follow its established conventions.The disagreement soon spilled into public. CPI state secretary Binoy Viswam criticised Vijayan's stand, while senior CPI leader C Divakaran went further and questioned Vijayan's authority to dismiss the demand. Divakaran also argued that Vijayan should have taken responsibility for the election defeat rather than becoming leader of the opposition.The CPM pushed back too. CPM state secretariat member C N Mohanan questioned the CPI's electoral strength and accused it of using pressure tactics against the larger ally.The dispute may appear procedural because the deputy leader's post is largely an organisational and parliamentary position. But its political significance lies elsewhere. The CPI has sought greater recognition after the LDF's defeat, while the CPM, as the dominant force in the alliance, remains the principal party responsible for its direction.The two parties have since tried to prevent the dispute from escalating further. But the episode illustrates a problem that often becomes sharper after an electoral defeat: who takes responsibility for the loss, and who gets to decide the course correction?Kerala's 2026 verdict completed a long retreat. West Bengal's Left Front had ruled continuously from 1977 until 2011, while Tripura remained under Left Front rule for 25 years before the BJP ended that run in 2018. Kerala subsequently became the Left's last major governing base.But the story of the Left's decline has not been the same everywhere. In West Bengal, the 2011 defeat ended 34 years of uninterrupted Left Front rule and the Communist parties have since struggled to recover their old electoral space. In Tripura, the BJP displaced the Left after 25 years in power and emerged as its principal rival. Kerala followed a different trajectory, with power traditionally alternating between the LDF and Congress-led UDF.That is what made the LDF's 2021 victory particularly significant. The Vijayan government returned for a second consecutive term, breaking Kerala's four-decade pattern of alternating governments and giving the Left something it no longer had elsewhere: a state where it could demonstrate that it remained capable not only of surviving, but of retaining power.The 2026 defeat is therefore different from Bengal and Tripura and cannot automatically be equated with the organisational collapse witnessed elsewhere. Yet the scale of the setback raises questions beyond normal anti-incumbency. The LDF was reduced from 94 seats to 35, while the UDF won 102. The CPI(M) also suffered defeats in areas traditionally associated with its organisation, including parts of Kannur. BJP candidates won three seats, Chathannoor, Nemom and Kazhakoottam, including constituencies that had been held by LDF leaders.The larger national trajectory has been just as stark. At its parliamentary peak in 2004, the Left parties together had 59 Lok Sabha MPs and provided crucial outside support to the first UPA government. Twenty-two years later, their presence in Parliament and across state governments is a fraction of what it was.The decline cannot be traced to a single election or a single cause. The Left has had to contend with the loss of old strongholds, changes in the nature of work and organised labour, the rise of powerful regional parties, the BJP's expansion into states where the Left once had substantial space, and the challenge of reaching a generation of voters with little memory of the Communist parties at the height of their political influence.Kerala had, for years, stood apart from that national decline. The 2026 result does not mean the Left's organisational base in the state has disappeared, but it has removed its last seat of state power and made the problems elsewhere much harder to ignore.With no Communist-led state government left, a diminished parliamentary presence, weaker conversion of student mobilisation into votes and visible friction among its own principal parties, the Left finds itself at one of its most difficult political moments.The challenge is no longer simply how to win the next election. It is whether the political space that once made the Communist movement a national force can still be reconstructed, and whether the Left can address its old fault lines while finding its place in a changing political landscape.
Article Summary: India's Left faces a deeper political challenge as electoral setbacks, internal tensions and shrinking influence converge. The Kerala defeat has left it without a state government, the CPM and CPI are publicly disagreeing over the way forward, and former chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan is facing a probe. Delhi university results have again exposed the gap between the Left’s visibility in student movements and its electoral reach.

Article Title: 'Wrong message to society': Rijiju attacks Rahul Gandhi over Gyanesh Kumar resignation demand
Article Text:
Rahul Gandhi had alleged that the 2024 Lok Sabha and assembly elections were “all rigged”.

NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Sunday attacked leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi over his criticism of the Election Commission and demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, saying such remarks would send a “wrong message to society”.Speaking to reporters, Rijiju said, “It is not appropriate to amplify Rahul Gandhi's remarks in the public sphere, as it would send the wrong message to society.”His remarks came days after Rahul Gandhi stepped up his attack on the Centre and the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Rahul had alleged that the 2024 Lok Sabha and assembly elections were “all rigged” and demanded the immediate resignation of Gyanesh Kumar.Addressing a press conference at the Congress headquarters on Thursday, the Congress leader accused the Election Commission of failing to protect voters’ rights and alleged that the electoral process had been compromised.“Mr Gyanesh Kumar must resign immediately. We are not going to let democracy be destroyed in India and sit silent, and the people responsible for this are going to be punished,” the Rae Bareli MP said.Rahul also referred to reports that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections on several occasions over decisions related to electoral-roll management and the SIR exercise.“The two Election Commissioners have done a wise thing, and I appreciate it,” he said. Rahul further alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah were “at the top of this conspiracy” and would be investigated. He also said Kumar should “turn approver”.“I can say with certainty that Indian elections -- 2024 Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha polls -- were all rigged,” Rahul said. He also linked his allegations over electoral rolls to the functioning of Parliament and other institutions.“From vote chori (vote theft), comes kanoon chori (law theft) and from that comes sanstha chori (institutional theft),” he said.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the reported objections reflected a disagreement over its final decisions.The poll panel said on Saturday that key decisions related to the SIR, including orders and schedules, were taken with the “unanimous approval” of all three commissioners.It also clarified that a letter sent to the Cabinet Secretary, which had drawn scrutiny, concerned the functioning of an officer on deputation to the ECI and was not related to any policy matter, ANI reported.The clarification came after an Indian Express report said that Sandhu and Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months on issues including voter registration, deletion and restoration of names, changes to Form 6 and access to electoral-roll databases.The ECI said the SIR order issued on June 24, 2025, covering all states and Union territories, was approved unanimously. It also said the schedules for subsequent phases were issued with the unanimous approval of the Commission.Earlier in the day, Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath also criticised the Congress and its allies over their attacks on the Election Commission and the SIR.“Congress and its allies should apologise to the constitutional institutions of the country and to the people for their actions,” Adityanath said.He said the SIR was not being conducted for the first time and pointed to earlier exercises carried out in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965-66 and 2003.“Despite all this, the kind of uproar that the Congress, Samajwadi Party, RJD and other parties have created over the SIR this time is extremely unfortunate,” he added.Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde also criticised the opposition over its demand for Kumar’s resignation. He alleged that Congress and its allies question the credibility of the Election Commission and EVMs after losing elections.“We are seeing what is happening. When the Congress wins in Telangana, Karnataka, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala, the Opposition does not comment on the Election Commission,” Shinde added.The political row comes amid continuing scrutiny of the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR. Opposition parties, including the Congress, CPI, CPI(M), Trinamool Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT), have demanded Kumar’s resignation.
Article Summary: Rahul Gandhi had alleged that the 2024 Lok Sabha and assembly elections were “all rigged” and demanded the immediate resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Rijiju: “It is not appropriate to amplify Rahul Gandhi's remarks in the public sphere, as it would send the wrong message to society”

Article Title: ‘There is no accountability’: Sonam Wangchuk seeks answers on Leh violence inquiry
Article Text:
Sonam Wangchuk questions inquiry into Leh violence

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk on Sunday questioned the status of the inquiry into the violence in Leh, saying a year had passed since the incidents and that those responsible were yet to be held accountable. He also raised concerns over the pending legal cases and the compensation for those who were killed.Wangchuk said he had travelled to Delhi to draw attention to the unresolved issues surrounding the violence and his subsequent imprisonment in Jodhpur."I had to come to Delhi to inform the country that a year has passed since those incidents in Ladakh, incidents that led to my own imprisonment in Jodhpur. I want to ask: what became of the findings of the inquiry commission set up regarding those incidents? When will the officials, the Governor, the Lieutenant Governor, and the Home Minister, who ordered such actions, provide answers? The issue remains unresolved. Those who were martyred have not yet received appropriate and dignified compensation. Legal cases are still pending against people, and many are left in a wretched state. There is no accountability."Protests demanding statehood for Ladakh and safeguards under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution turned violent on September 24, 2025, leaving four people dead and several others injured. The Union Territory administration subsequently ordered a judicial inquiry into the incident.Wangchuk was detained under the National Security Act (NSA) two days after the violence and was released in March this year.On the Election Commission of India row, Wangchuk said he supported organisations and leaders raising concerns over the electoral process and accountability, while acknowledging that he could not personally participate in every movement."I always extend my moral support to all organizations and leaders raising such issues, issues that are entirely valid, such as cleaning up the election process and ensuring accountability. However, it is not possible for me to personally join every single movement. I hope the entire country will join in demanding this accountability to build a clean, transparent democracy."The remarks come amid a political row over reported objections by two Election Commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Opposition parties have demanded action against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a halt to the SIR exercise and fresh elections in states where polls have already been held.The BJP, however, has defended the Election Commission, with party spokesperson Sambit Patra saying that dissent within the poll panel was a sign of a “vibrant democracy”.
Article Summary: Sonam Wangchuk questions the status of the inquiry into the violence in Leh. He also raised concerns over the pending legal cases and the compensation for those who were killed. Protests demanding statehood for Ladakh turned violent on September 24, 2025, leaving four people dead.

Article Title: NPF gets most, BJP second as 111 MPs, MLAs switch parties since 2022: ADR
Article Text:
At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties after being elected between 2022 and 2026

NPF received most lawmakers, BJP second

Who were the 29 lawmakers who joined BJP?

Nagaland, West Bengal account for major share of cases

NDPP, AITC and Congress recorded most exits

Not all 111 cases were individual defections

ADR cautions that list may not be exhaustive

NEW DELHI: At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties after being elected between 2022 and 2026, according to an analysis by the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) and National Election Watch (NEW). The report, released on September 24, covers elections and by-elections held during the period and includes 26 Lok Sabha MPs, seven Rajya Sabha MPs and 78 MLAs.The cases span 17 states and Union Territories, with Nagaland recording the highest number at 32, followed by West Bengal with 20, Telangana with nine, and Goa and Punjab with eight each. Maharashtra and Meghalaya recorded six cases each, Manipur five, Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat four each, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan two each, while Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi recorded one each.Of the 111 lawmakers, 32 joined the Naga People's Front (NPF), accounting for 29 per cent of the total. The BJP received 29, or 26 per cent, followed by the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) with 20, or 18 per cent.The Congress received nine lawmakers, or 8 per cent, while Shiv Sena received eight, or 7 per cent. NPP received six, or 5 per cent, and the People's Party of Arunachal (PPA) received four, or 4 per cent.Together, NPF, BJP and NCPI accounted for 81 of the 111 lawmakers, or 73 per cent.The NPF's figure was largely linked to the political realignment involving the Nationalist Democratic Progressive Party (NDPP) and NPF in Nagaland. ADR classifies party mergers separately from individual defections, making the distinction important when reading the overall figures.Of the 29 lawmakers listed as having joined the BJP, seven were Rajya Sabha MPs and 22 were MLAs. No Lok Sabha MP in the ADR dataset moved to the BJP.The seven Rajya Sabha MPs were originally elected from the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP): Swati Maliwal, Ashok Mittal, Harbhajan Singh, Raghav Chadha, Sandeep Kumar Pathak, Vikramjit Singh Sahney and Rajinder Gupta. The seven AAP MPs subsequently joined the BJP in April 2026.Among the MLAs were eight Congress legislators from Goa, four Congress legislators from Gujarat and two from Himachal Pradesh. The report also lists five JD(U) MLAs from Manipur as having moved to the BJP.Other BJP entrants included Samajwadi Party MLA Manoj Kumar Pandey from Uttar Pradesh, Congress MLA Nirmala Sapre from Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka MLA G Janardhan Reddy, whose Kalyana Rajya Pragathi Paksha (KRPP) merged with the BJP, according to the ADR analysis.Four Gujarat Congress MLAs, CJ Chavda, Arjun Modhwadia, Arvind Ladani and Chirag Patel, resigned, joined the BJP and subsequently contested by-elections.Nagaland recorded 32 cases, all involving MLAs. The cases were largely linked to the NDPP-NPF realignment, with 25 representatives originally elected from the NDPP among those who changed parties and 32 lawmakers joining the NPF.West Bengal recorded 20 cases, all involving Lok Sabha MPs. All 20 were originally elected on AITC tickets and subsequently moved to the NCPI, according to the analysis. The MPs have claimed a merger with the NCPI, with the matter pending before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.Telangana recorded nine cases, all involving MLAs originally elected from the BRS, while Congress emerged as the principal recipient. Goa recorded eight cases involving Congress MLAs who moved to the BJP. Punjab also recorded eight cases, including six Rajya Sabha members and two MLAs.Maharashtra recorded six cases, all involving Lok Sabha MPs elected from Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) who subsequently moved to Shiv Sena led by Eknath Shinde. Meghalaya recorded six MLA cases, while Manipur recorded five.Among the parties from which lawmakers moved, NDPP recorded the highest number of exits, with 25, or 23 per cent of the total. AITC followed with 20, or 18 per cent, while Congress accounted for 19, or 17 per cent.BRS recorded nine exits, or 8 per cent. AAP and NCP each accounted for seven, or 6 per cent, while Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) accounted for six, or 5 per cent. JD(U) recorded five, or 5 per cent, and NPP four, or 4 per cent.Together, NDPP, AITC and Congress accounted for 64 of the 111 lawmakers who changed parties, or 58 per cent.ADR's analysis divides the 111 cases into four categories based on how the change took place.The first covers individual switches or defections, where a legislator voluntarily leaves one party and joins another without resigning from the House.The second covers party mergers, where the original party or a substantial section of its legislative wing formally merges with another party, such as the NDPP-NPF case in Nagaland.The third covers resignation followed by a by-election, where a legislator resigns from the Assembly or Parliament, joins another party and subsequently contests and wins a by-election.The fourth covers disqualification followed by a by-election, where a member is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, later joins another party and wins the seat again through a by-election.ADR also noted that recent defections had been associated with the fall of governments in some State Assemblies.ADR and NEW said they made every effort to identify and include all relevant cases but cautioned that the list may not be exhaustive because of the lack of systematically maintained and readily accessible official data on lawmakers changing political parties. Other relevant cases may therefore not have been included.The previous ADR report on MPs and MLAs who changed parties was released on September 9, 2021, and covered the period from 2014 to 2021.
Article Summary: At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties between 2022 and 2026. Nagaland recorded the highest number at 32, followed by West Bengal with 20, Telangana with nine, and Goa and Punjab with eight each. Of the 111 lawmakers, 32 joined the Naga People's Front (NPF), accounting for 29 per cent of the total.

Article Title: Punjab school holiday September 28: Schools and government offices to remain closed for Bhagat Singh Jayanti
Article Text:
September 28 holiday: Punjab schools to remain closed for Shaheed Bhagat Singh Jayanti

Punjab school holiday September 28

:

Why schools will remain closed on September 28

Bhagat Singh Jayanti and educational institutions

Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev

September 28 holiday in Punjab

Schools across Punjab will remain closed on September 28 on the occasion of Shaheed Bhagat Singh Jayanti. The state government has declared a holiday to mark the birth anniversary of freedom fighter Bhagat Singh, with the closure applicable to educational institutions across the state.The holiday will also apply to government offices in Punjab. Students, teachers and staff will therefore not have regular school activities on September 28. The day is observed every year to remember Bhagat Singh and his contribution to India's freedom movement.September 28 marks the birth anniversary of Bhagat Singh, who was born in Punjab on September 28, 1907. He became one of the prominent figures associated with India's freedom struggle against British rule and was involved in the revolutionary movement during the period.Bhagat Singh was associated with the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA), which was involved in revolutionary activities during India's struggle for independence. His role in the freedom movement has made his birth anniversary an important occasion in the state.Schools and other educational institutions observe Bhagat Singh Jayanti through various activities.Programmes held to mark the occasion can include speeches, discussions and essay-writing competitions focused on his life and contribution to India's freedom movement.The September 28 holiday means such regular academic activities will not be conducted in schools on the day of the state-declared closure. Institutions may organise commemorative programmes on another working day according to their schedules.Bhagat Singh, along with fellow revolutionaries Rajguru and Sukhdev, was executed on March 23, 1931. Their deaths are remembered in connection with India's freedom struggle.Bhagat Singh's birth anniversary is observed annually, with educational institutions and public organisations using the occasion to remember his role in the country's independence movement. The day also provides an opportunity for students to learn about the historical events and revolutionary activities associated with the freedom struggle.The September 28 holiday will cover schools and other educational institutions across Punjab, along with government offices. Students and parents can plan their schedules accordingly, while schools will resume their regular academic activities after the declared holiday.The closure has been announced specifically for Shaheed Bhagat Singh Jayanti, marking his birth anniversary on September 28.
Article Summary: Punjab schools to remain closed on September 28 for Shaheed Bhagat Singh Jayanti. The state government has declared a holiday to mark the birth anniversary of the freedom fighter. Students, teachers and staff will not have regular school activities on the day.

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Saturday said all decisions taken on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously, while announcing measures to simplify the process for voters facing notices over discrepancies.The clarification comes amid row over report that claimed differences within the EC over SIR of electoral rolls."In the recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions including SIR across the country. The order for the SIR issued on 24.6.2025 for all the States/UTs, starting with Bihar, followed by West Bengal and 30 other States/UTs was issued with the unanimous approval of the Commission. The same has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India vide its order dated 27.5.2026. The schedule for SIR for 12 States and UTs was issued on 27.10.2025 and those for 19 States/UTs was issued on 14.05.2026 with the unanimous approval of the Commission. The final figure of number of electors will be known only after final publication in the remaining 12 states of Phase-III," the poll body said in a statement.At a meeting held on Saturday, the Commission decided that voters who receive notices during the ongoing SIR over being unmapped or having logical discrepancies will not ordinarily have to appear before the electoral registration officer (ERO).Booth-level officers (BLOs) will visit their homes to collect documents and upload them on ECINet for the ERO to decide.Hearings will be held only in exceptional cases, preferably online. An adult family member can also attend a hearing on behalf of the elector if authorised. The Commission said facilities for online hearings would be strengthened.The Commission also directed district election officers to set up help desks and special camps for people living in night shelters, labourers, poor people and homeless persons, depending on local requirements.The EC said SIR has been completed in 20 states and Union territories, including Bihar and West Bengal. It said voters whose names were left out during or after the exercise, as well as young and first-time voters, can apply to the concerned ERO for inclusion through continuous updation. Chief Electoral Officers (CEOs), DEOs and EROs have been directed to launch a special enrolment drive.The Commission also clarified that a letter sent to the Cabinet Secretary was not related to any policy decision concerning the Commission or its IT division, but concerned the functioning of an officer on deputation to the EC.It said work redistribution orders issued by the officer were not implemented after directions from two Commissioners, and oversight of the IT division by the Deputy Election Commissioner was never withdrawn.The EC said field officers have role-based access to the ECINet system based on their statutory powers. A committee headed by a senior Deputy Election Commissioner and including an independent IIT/IIIT expert will review the system for compliance with relevant laws and rules.The Commission also said future initiatives involving IT modules and portals would be discussed by the Committee of Officers before being placed for approval.The Commission extended the deadline for filing claims and objections in Delhi till October 30, following a request from the Delhi CEO. The deadline for disposal of notices and claims and objections has been extended till November 30.In Maharashtra, the deadline for filing claims and objections has been extended till October 12, while their disposal will continue till November 10.The Commission further said the SIR order issued on June 24, 2025, covering all states and UTs and subsequently implemented in phases, had received unanimous approval. It added that the Supreme Court upheld the order on May 27, 2026.In Goa, the EC said BLOs had been directed to visit voters left out of the rolls and collect their forms. Of 97 such voters, 81 have already filled Form 6 for inclusion.The Commission also directed that agendas for its meetings be circulated in advance and minutes issued, while requiring officers' annual performance reports to be completed by December 31 each year. It further said Commission approval would be required for official foreign trips and that directions issued by Commissioners to officers must be complied with.
Article Summary: The Election Commission on Saturday said all decisions taken on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously. The Commission also announced measures to simplify the process for voters facing notices over discrepancies. The clarification comes amid row over report that claimed differences within the EC.

Article Title: As Trump hugs Xi and plugs Sharif, India feels the squeeze
Article Text:
Trump’s outreach to Xi and praise for Sharif come as India faces a more transactional US relationship

TOI correspondent from Washington:

The clearest sign yet of a widening US-India diplomatic rift came this weekend from the White House and the United Nations, where India was denouncing Pakistan for what it called a litany of “falsehoods” and “deceit,” even as US President Donald Trump appeared to give those very claims a presidential imprimatur.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had used his UN General Assembly address to revive Islamabad’s account of the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, crediting Trump with a “timely intervention” that, he said, prevented a wider war. On Friday night, shortly after China’s President Xi Jinping had departed for Beijing, Trump posted an 87-second excerpt of Sharif’s speech on Truth Social without comment. The clip included Sharif’s praise of Trump and Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir.The timing was striking. India had just exercised its Right of Reply, with First Secretary Petal Gahlot accusing Islamabad of peddling “falsehoods” and “deceit” and describing Pakistan as a “puppet” regime. New Delhi has also rejected Trump’s repeated assertion that he mediated the cessation of hostilities in May 2025, saying the fighting was halted after direct military-to-military communication between India and Pakistan.For India, however, the larger concern may be less about one Truth Social post than about a pattern. The Xi visit to Washington this week appeared to underscore how dramatically the strategic geometry of US foreign policy has shifted. Rather than organizing its Asia policy principally around building India as a counterweight to China – a two-decade old Washington objective that resulting in an “Indo-Pacific” focused QUAD – the Trump White House increasingly appears willing to deal with Beijing as a peer whose cooperation is indispensable, and whose confrontation carries costs Trump is reluctant to incur.Following the Xi visit, Washington and Beijing extended their trade truce and agreed on tariff reductions covering $30 billion of less-sensitive goods in each direction, according reports in the Chinese media. They also operationalized bilateral boards on trade and investment and agreed to pursue an artificial-intelligence dialogue.Analysts say none of this amounts to a formal US-China condominium, and deep disagreements over Taiwan, technology, trade and strategic competition remain. But the emerging arrangement has prompted comparisons with a de facto G-2: Washington and Beijing managing their rivalry directly while other powers, including India, find themselves having to adjust to decisions made in a room in which they are not present.“One totally unsurprising consequence of this US-China trade truce is that Trump is not even thinking about implementing the Lindsey Graham Russia sanctions legislation he just signed, which would have required penalizing China's support for Russia's war machine,” Tom Malinowski a former New Jersey lawmaker noted, even as Republicans close to Trump have been champing at the bit to punish New Delhi. The Graham bill, signed by Trump on Sept. 18, gives the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian crude or natural gas under specified conditions. The law specifically covers countries among the five largest Russian oil or gas importers that make new purchases, as well as countries identified among the top facilitators of sanctions evasion.India is plainly exposed to that provision, as is China. Yet the contrast in Trump’s handling of the two relationships has become difficult for New Delhi to ignore: Beijing is being courted into a new economic accommodation even as India faces the prospect of punitive trade action.The message was reinforced this week by a senior State Department official who said the Graham law gives Trump “a new tool in his toolbox,” while emphasizing that its use is not automatic. The official pointed to a broad national-security waiver but added that Washington expects India to help the US end the Ukraine war.More revealing was the official's description of what Washington now wants from India: not necessarily strategic alignment against China, but access to the enormous Indian energy market. “We are looking to also become a huge source of India's energy needs,” the official was quoted as saying, pointing to expanding US hydrocarbon exports and urging faster diversification away from Russian supplies.All this is consequential because for two decades the bipartisan American strategy had been to help India acquire the economic, military and technological heft to balance China's rise. As recently as May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who will be back in New Delhi in October, was describing India as one of America's most important strategic partners, while US officials continued to characterize New Delhi as a critical Indo-Pacific counterweight.The language now coming from Washington is noticeably more transactional.For New Delhi, the resulting unease is not simply about tariffs or Pakistan. It is about whether a strategic partnership painstakingly built across successive administrations is being replaced by a transactional relationship in which China is too powerful to punish, Pakistan is useful to cultivate, and India is expected to accommodate. And as New Delhi watched Washington kiss up to Beijing as an indispensable peer and embrace a country New Delhi views as a terrorism sponsor, the strategic space India once occupied in the American imagination appeared to be shrinking.
Article Summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had used his UN General Assembly address to revive Islamabad’s account of the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict. On Friday night, shortly after Xi Jinping had departed for Beijing, Trump posted an 87-second excerpt of Sharif's speech on Truth Social without comment. India had just exercised its Right of Reply, with First Secretary Petal Gahlot accusing Islamabad of peddling “falsehoods” and “deceit”

NEW DELHI: Those applying for fresh enrolment as electors through Form 6 in locations other than the 12 states and UTs where special intensive revision (SIR) is currently underway will no longer need to attach a declaration mapping themselves or their relative to the electoral rolls from the last SIR.In the states and UTs where SIR is going on, Form 6 will continue to be accompanied by a mandatory declaration by the applicant listing their or their relatives' electoral rolls details from the last SIR, apart from their father's, mother's and spouse's names and their respective EPIC numbers, if available.A statement put out by the three-member Election Commission Saturday justified the continued requirement of new electors to submit the declaration along with Form 6 as part of SIR, saying "the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Supreme Court ".For the non-SIR period, the forms applicable as per the Registration of Electors Rules 1960 will be used, the commission added. NEW DELHI: Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah on Sunday flagged off India’s first LNG-powered train in Gujarat and launched a series of railway projects worth more than Rs 1,542 crore at Sabarmati The LNG-based train uses a diesel-LNG dual-fuel system, with two 1,400 HP Driving Power Cars at the Sabarmati Integrated Coaching Depot converted to run on both fuels. Kavach is designed to help prevent train collisions, protect against overspeeding and reduce risks linked to human error.An automatic block signalling system has also been introduced across 122.57 km of railway sections between Sabarmati-Kalol-Bhandu Motidau and Sabarmati-Sanand-Jakhwada at a cost of around Rs 118.83 crore. NEW DELHI: Elections are, by their very nature, a contest.Political parties fight for ground, candidates wage fierce campaigns and voters ultimately decide whom to trust with their mandate.Through it all, the Election Commission is meant to stand apart and monitor the process. Its role is to frame the rules, enforce them fairly and ensure that the contest remains even-handed.Yet, in recent days, the spotlight has moved away from those fighting the election and towards the institution meant to referee it.The players are no longer the only ones under scrutiny. Increasingly, the referee itself has become the subject of the debate.A report in The Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi repeatedly raised objections with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over decisions and communications that they said were issued without their knowledge or approval.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the episode points to a breakdown in its functioning. It has maintained that differences of opinion are a normal part of institutional deliberation and that all final decisions of the Commission have been unanimous.That leaves a larger constitutional question at the heart of the controversy: how is India's election watchdog actually supposed to function?Is the Chief Election Commissioner the boss of the Election Commission, or simply the first among three equals? What happens when the three commissioners disagree? And why has the law governing their appointment become a subject of such intense controversy?On September 23, The Indian Express reported that Sandhu and Joshi had, on multiple occasions, objected to decisions and communications they said were taken or issued without their prior knowledge.According to the report, the two commissioners recorded such objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months.The issues reportedly ranged from changes to electoral forms and access to the voter database to the allocation of work within the Commission and the filing of appeals involving electoral rolls.The report has since triggered a wider debate over whether the Election Commission's three members are exercising their powers collectively, as the law envisages, or whether the CEC has acquired a greater role in practice.According to the Indian Express report, the concerns raised by Sandhu and Joshi covered several aspects of the Commission's functioning.Taken together, the reported objections raise a question that goes beyond any individual decision: how does a three-member constitutional body exercise collective authority when its members do not initially agree?The Election Commission strongly rejected the suggestion that its internal differences amount to a breakdown in decision-making, and added that all official orders and administrative directions had been issued unanimously."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the ECI said in a statement."In recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms, including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year," the poll body added.It also criticised the media report, saying that highlighting specific internal notes over a period of 10 months gives only one part of the picture."Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said.The disagreement, therefore, is not simply over whether commissioners have expressed reservations. It is over what those reservations mean for the functioning of the institution as a whole.This is where the 2023 law becomes important.Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, provides that the Commission may, by unanimous decision, regulate how its business is conducted and allocate work among the CEC and the other Election Commissioners.It also says that, as far as possible, the Commission's business should be transacted unanimously.But it makes an important provision for situations in which consensus is not possible.If the CEC and the other Election Commissioners differ on a matter, the issue is to be decided according to the opinion of the majority.In other words, the statutory framework does not make the CEC an executive superior to the other two commissioners. The three constitute the Commission collectively, while the CEC is the "first among equals".The CEC can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the CEC's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners.Where the three disagree, the majority view is the deciding view.The controversy now centres on whether some of the decisions cited in the recent report were, in practice, implemented despite objections from the other two commissioners, and if so, how that squares with the statutory scheme governing the Commission's decision-making.The current controversy also brings back an older and deeper question: Who should appoint the people who conduct India's elections?In March 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament had not yet enacted a law governing appointments to the Election Commission, despite Article 324 of the Constitution envisaging such a framework.Until Parliament enacted such a law, a Constitution bench prescribed an interim selection mechanism comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.The court stressed that an independent Election Commission was essential for democracy and observed that those entrusted with conducting elections must be insulated from executive influence.Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.But the new law changed the composition of the selection committee.Instead of the Chief Justice of India, it provided for a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The committee therefore consists of the Prime Minister, a Union minister nominated by him and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.The opposition has alleged that the 2023 Act gives the executive “overwhelming” control over the appointment of Election Commissioners. The government, meanwhile, has defended the law and its institutional framework.The dispute has now reached the Supreme Court, where a challenge to the validity of the appointment law produced a split verdict.A two-judge SC bench differed over whether the matter should immediately be referred to a Constitution bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma disagreed on that question, although both agreed that the matter should ultimately be placed before the Chief Justice of India for consideration by a larger bench.They also agreed that sending the case first to a three-judge bench would be of "little worth" and could further delay a final determination of the constitutional questions involved. The matter is likely to be heard by a 5-judge bench soon.The issue is vital as it extends beyond the current dispute inside the Election Commission. It touches a larger institutional question: How independent should the body conducting India's elections be from the executive, and what safeguards should govern the appointment of those who head it?The latest controversy has also acquired a political dimension, with opposition parties preparing fresh notices seeking the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.According to media reports, the notices, being drafted and vetted by experts, are expected to be submitted in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha next week. The proposed notices are expected to include issues raised in the Indian Express report.This would not be the opposition's first attempt.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan rejected an earlier notice seeking Kumar's removal. That notice had been signed by 130 Lok Sabha members and 63 Rajya Sabha members and alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the conduct of the SIR exercise.Separately, a notice submitted by 73 opposition MPs in the Rajya Sabha on April 24 seeking Kumar's removal remains pending in the Upper House.But removing a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution provides that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court".The same protection is incorporated into Section 11(2) of the 2023 Act.The other Election Commissioners enjoy a different safeguard: they cannot be removed from office except on the recommendation of the CEC.The higher threshold for removing a CEC is intended to protect the office from arbitrary or politically motivated removal.The removal process is rooted in the constitutional procedure applicable to Supreme Court judges.Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.The current structure of the Election Commission is itself the product of an institutional evolution.When the ECI was established in 1950, it was a single-member body, with the Chief Election Commissioner as its sole member.It became a three-member body for the first time in 1989, but that arrangement was short-lived. In January 1990, the VP Singh government reverted the Commission to a single-member structure.The system changed again in October 1993, when the PV Narasimha Rao government appointed MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy as Election Commissioners alongside CEC TN Seshan.Seshan challenged the appointments in the Supreme Court, arguing that the addition of commissioners diluted the authority of the CEC.In its 1995 judgment, a Constitution bench upheld the multi-member structure.The court made clear that the CEC was not institutionally superior to the other Election Commissioners. The three were intended to function collectively, with differences being resolved through the decision-making mechanism of the Commission.That judgment established the broad institutional framework that exists today.The Election Commission is not designed as a hierarchy in which one person commands and two others merely assist. Nor is it simply three independent offices operating in parallel. It is a constitutional body meant to function collectively.The law provides for unanimity where possible and a majority where consensus fails.The CEC occupies the position of first among equals, rather than that of a superior authority.The significance of the current controversy, therefore, lies not merely in the existence of disagreements within the Commission. Differences are inevitable in any institution exercising such enormous constitutional responsibility.The larger question is what happens after those differences arise: whether they remain part of an internal deliberative process, as the ECI maintains, or whether they reflect a deeper dispute over how collective authority is being exercised.The credibility of an election does not rest only on the final tally of votes.It also rests on whether voters believe that the rules were applied fairly, the institutions enforcing them remained above the contest and the process was conducted without favour or hidden influence.The Election Commission, therefore, carries a burden that goes beyond administering polls: it must command confidence across the political spectrum and among voters themselves. Any perception that the referee is divided, opaque or partisan can cast a shadow over the process, even when the electoral machinery continues to function formally within the law.In the end, public trust is not built merely by declaring an election free and fair; it is built by ensuring that voters have little reason to doubt that verdict.
Article Summary: Joshi and Sandhu objected to changes to Form 6, the application citizens use to register as new electors, without following due process. They also raised concerns about whether statutory authorities responsible for maintaining electoral rolls had complete access to voter data on the ERONet portal. Joshi flagged what he described as the "gradual centralisation of the electoral roll database"

Article Title: After meeting, EC says officials will visit homes of those sent notices

ECINET software to be audited after complaints​

NEW DELHI: A full meeting of the Election Commission of India on Saturday - the first after reports of alleged internal differences - decided to exempt electors who have got notices for being unmapped to the last SIR or over logical discrepancies, from hearings by electoral registration officer (ERO) or assistant EROs. Instead, EROs and AEROs will visit homes of such electors to collect documents that would then be uploaded to ECINet for a final decision by the ERO.The EC also agreed to an independent audit of ECINET software though it rejected allegations that EROs were being locked out."Only in exceptional circumstances, as decided by the ERO, hearing will be held, preferably online. Any adult member of the family can be authorised by the elector to attend the hearing on their behalf, if required," the EC said in a statement after the meeting attended by CEC Gyanesh Kumar and election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.EC also agreed to an independent audit of ECINET software even as it rejected allegations that booth-level officers and EROs were being kept out.Facilities for online hearing will be strengthened, while DEOs will create enough help desks and hold special camps for the poor, labourers, homeless people, and those in night shelters.The relief for electors who received notices under SIR follows criticism from affected voters and opposition that genuine citizens are being inconvenienced by discrepancies flagged by ECINET.These include name or gender mismatch; less than a 15-year gap with a parent; less than a 40-year gap with a grandparent; being one of six progeny mapped to the same parent; and less than a nine-month gap between siblings.Until now, notice recipients had to appear before the ERO at the specified time and place with documents proving eligibility to remain on the rolls. With large numbers of notices in states like Delhi, including to prominent persons, many said citizens were forced to run around to retain voting rights.EC has also denied reports that field officers were locked out of ECINET, saying role-based access exists, but agreed to an independent audit. A senior DEC-led panel will review ECINET to double-check that it complies with the provisions of the Acts and rules and submit a report to EC.
Article Summary: EC also agreed to an independent audit of ECINET software even as it rejected allegations that booth-level officers and EROs were being kept out.Facilities for online hearing will be strengthened, while DEOs will create enough help desks and hold special camps.

Article Title: Higher EPF wage limit: Monthly PF contributions rise to Rs 3,917
Article Text:
EPFO wage ceiling hike

NEW DELHI: With EPFO increasing the mandatory wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 a month to Rs 25,000, employees will now contribute Rs 3,000 (at 12% contribution of Rs 25,000 wage) towards their PF savings from Rs 1,800 earlier, govt said in a set of FAQs released. This will be along with a contribution of Rs 917 by employers (at 3.67%), up from Rs 550, taking the mandatory monthly PF contributions to Rs 3,917.In addition, Rs 2,083 - an 8.3% contribution from employers' share - will now go towards the pension kitty from earlier Rs 1,250. On Sept 17, govt increased EPFO wage ceiling to bring one crore additional workers into the social security net as minimum wages in at least seven states and UTs - Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Haryana, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Uttarakhand - have crossed the Rs 15,000 threshold.In the case of an employee with a monthly wage of Rs 20,000, the mandatory PF contribution will be Rs 3,134 - the employee share Rs 2,400 and the employer share Rs 734, with an additional Rs 1,666 going towards EPS from employer's share. But if an employee earns, say, Rs 35,000 a month, the mandatory PF contribution will be Rs 6,000 (Rs 3,000 from employee and employers each), with no amount going towards pension as EPS is available only to those whose wages do not exceed the EPFO wage ceiling.The retirement savings agency said the new regime kicked in from Sept 17 and asked employers to review contractor compliance, wherever contract labour is engaged, and update its payroll systems.Allaying employee fears of attempts to pass on the contribution by deducting more from salaries, it said an employer's statutory contribution cannot simply be treated as an employee deduction merely by describing it as part of CTC.While the move will likely increase compliance costs for small and medium enterprises, the potential costs due to the rise in the wage ceiling can be partly offset by the incentive of up to Rs 3,000 per month for every additional employment created under PM Viksit Bharat Rojgar Yojana.
Article Summary: EPFO increasing mandatory wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 a month to Rs 25,000. Employees will now contribute Rs 3,000 towards their PF savings from Rs 1,800 earlier. This will be along with a contribution of Rs 917 by employers (at 3.67%), up from Rs 550.

Article Title: PM Modi recalls 2016 surgical strikes on Mann Ki Baat, says terrorism will get decisive response
Article Text:
File photo: PM Modi in 'Mann Ki Baat'

Other highlights from Mann Ki Baat

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday recalled the 2016 surgical strikes carried out by the Indian Army across the Line of Control (LoC), saying India has made it clear that terrorism will be met with a “strong and decisive response”.Addressing the 138th episode of his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat , PM Modi said the surgical strikes, carried out on September 28-29, 2016, demonstrated India's resolve to respond to cross-border terrorism.“A major historical achievement of India is set to complete 10 years in just a day—the surgical strike. Ten years ago, on September 28–29, 2016, the Indian Army conducted a surgical strike on terrorist hideouts in PoJK. The world was astonished by the manner in which our brave soldiers crossed the Line of Control (LoC) to take action against terrorism,” he said.PM Modi said the operation had demonstrated a new approach to India's counter-terrorism policy.“The surgical strike boldly demonstrated a new example of India's counter-terrorism policy to the entire world. It served as our decisive response to the long-standing suffering India had endured due to terrorist attacks,” he said.“India has made it clear that terrorism will be met with a strong and decisive response,” PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also referred to the Balakot airstrike and Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message in response to terrorism.“Over the past decade, from the Balakot airstrike to 'Operation Sindoor', India has repeatedly sent a clear message: if terrorists dare to cast a hostile eye on India, they will face a befitting response,” he said.PM Modi also asserted that India was following a policy of “zero tolerance against terrorism”.The surgical strikes were carried out in response to the 2016 Uri terror attack, with the Indian Army targeting terror launch pads across the LoC.The Prime Minister also referred to the ongoing Census exercise, describing it as a “national responsibility” and saying every citizen had a role to play. He said the first phase of the Census was almost complete across all states and Union territories, with information on more than 32 crore families already recorded. He urged people to actively participate in the exercise and make use of the online enumeration facility.With October 2 approaching, PM Modi also highlighted cleanliness initiatives being carried out by communities across the country and recalled Mahatma Gandhi's emphasis on cleanliness.“October 2nd is just a few days away; it is the birth anniversary of Revered Bapu. Bapu gave us many mantras for life; cleanliness is one of them,” he said.PM Modi cited examples of youngsters cleaning a river in Madhya Pradesh, restoring old stepwells and wells in Andhra Pradesh, volunteers cleaning Mumbai beaches and young people in Delhi spreading awareness about waste segregation. He also mentioned students and local residents in West Bengal who were cleaning picnic spots.“One thing is clearly evident in all these efforts: it started with one person, then others joined in and the caravan grew. This is public participation,” PM Modi said.“Cleanliness is also the most beautiful tribute we can pay to Bapu,” he added.PM Modi also spoke about the fight against narcotics and said young people were coming together to spread awareness against drug addiction through the Nasha Mukt Yuva Abhiyan. He said millions of young people had taken a pledge to stay away from drugs and had also taken responsibility for spreading the message among others.The Prime Minister also recalled the history of the Somnath temple, saying those who sought to erase India's identity by destroying it ultimately had no existence. He said the temple continued to stand in its grandeur by the sea, blessing India with immortality.During the broadcast, PM Modi also paid tribute to late VHP leader Ashok Singhal on his birth anniversary, recalling his contribution to the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and describing his life as that of an ascetic who remained engaged with society.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi recalled the 2016 surgical strikes carried out by the Indian Army across the Line of Control (LoC) He said the operation demonstrated India's resolve to respond to cross-border terrorism. PM Modi also referred to the Balakot airstrike and Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message.

NEW DELHI: India and Canada are looking to take their bilateral relationship to a “higher level”, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said after meeting Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.“Always a pleasure to meet FM @AnitaAnandMP of Canada #UNGA81 A productive discussion as we prepare to take the relationship to a higher level,” Jaishankar said in a post on X on Saturday.The meeting comes as New Delhi and Ottawa work to rebuild ties and advance negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. Article Text:
Tamil Nadu CM C Joseph Vijay

What the exemption means

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the exemption of the Public (Law and Order) Department from the RTI Act? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu government led by CM C Joseph Vijay has exempted the Public (Law and Order) Department from the ambit of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, classifying it as an Intelligence and Security Organisation under Section 24(4) of the law.A Gazette notification issued by the state government places the department under the exemption framework applicable to intelligence and security organisations. The move means information held by the department will generally be outside the scope of RTI requests, subject to the statutory exceptions under the Act.The Public (Law and Order) Department deals with matters concerning policing, public order and law-and-order administration and RTI Act is a law to provide for setting out the practical regime of right to information for citizens wherein they can secure access to information under the control of public authorities.This exemption could therefore affect RTI requests seeking information relating to communal incidents, political agitations, police actions and other law-and-order matters handled by the department.The statement reads, "Gazette notification dated September 21, 2026, issued by the Human Resources Management Department, the Governor, exercising powers under Section 24(4) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, has specified the Public (Law and Order) Department as an "Intelligence and Security Organization" established by the Tamil Nadu government, "for which the said Act shall not apply."However, Section 24 of the RTI Act does not provide a blanket exemption. Even organisations covered by the provision are required to provide information relating to allegations of corruption and human-rights violations, subject to the procedure prescribed under the law.Tamil Nadu has previously used the provision to exclude organisations including the Tamil Nadu State Vigilance Commission and the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu government exempts Public (Law and Order) Department from the Right to Information (RTI) Act, classifying it as an Intelligence and Security Organisation. The move means information held by the department will generally be outside the scope of RTI requests, subject to the statutory exceptions under the Act.

Khera said.Khera alleged that the SIR exercise was based on an "illegally changed" Form 6 and questioned the validity of elections conducted in Bengal and Bihar on the basis of the exercise."The entire SIR is based on a Form 6 that was changed illegally. The SIR that arose from that illegal form has also become illegal. The elections held in Bengal and Bihar based on that illegal SIR have also become illegal. Did we get an answer on this?" he said.The controversy centres on the requirement for new voters to provide details linking themselves or their parents or grandparents to electoral rolls from the previous SIR.According to Indian Express reports, Election Commissioners Joshi and Sandhu had objected to incorporating the requirement into Form 6, arguing that the statutory form could not be altered without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.The Election Commission, however, has maintained that there was "no change" to Form 6 and that the SIR-related requirement was an additional declaration prescribed under its SIR orders. NEW DELHI: India has called for a global system that ensures countries sharing pathogens and biological resources during a health emergency also get timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, medicines and technologies developed from them.The demand was made at the UN High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response in New York, where India stressed that the credibility of the WHO Pandemic Agreement would depend on a fair Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.Union health secretary Punya Salila Srivastava said countries contributing pathogens should receive the benefits arising from their use, while respecting national sovereignty. She also said ongoing negotiations on the PABS system should not be prejudged and that implementation should take into account national circumstances and capacities.Drawing on its experience during Covid-19, India also called for digital public infrastructure to be recognised as a global public good, citing its role in disease surveillance, vaccination, risk communication, supply chains and continuity of health services during the pandemic.India highlighted its contribution during Covid, saying it supplied 300 million vaccine doses to around 100 countries and two UN entities, besides providing medical assistance to more than 150 countries.At the meeting, India also outlined measures to strengthen pandemic preparedness, including expanding laboratory networks, emergency coordination, the health workforce, stockpiles and clinical care capacity.The WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, is aimed at strengthening global preparedness for future pandemics. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for urgent completion of negotiations on the PABS system, saying delays could affect the world's ability to respond to future pandemics.India stressed that pandemic preparedness must remain rooted in national health systems and domestic financing, with international assistance complementing national efforts. It also called for equity and global solidarity to remain central to preparations for future outbreaks.
Article Summary: India has called for a global system that ensures countries sharing pathogens and biological resources during a health emergency get timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, medicines and technologies developed from them. Article Title: Bangladeshi woman says Bengaluru hospital withheld husband’s body for 8 days over Rs 35L bill; High Commission intervenes

A 26-year-old Bangladeshi woman has alleged that a leading private hospital in Bengaluru withheld her husband’s body for eight days over unpaid dues of Rs 35.79 lakh and retained her passport after he died during treatment. She received the body on Saturday after seeking help from Bangladesh High Commission. The hospital confirmed releasing the body but did not respond to her allegations. The hospital later said the patient had undergone critical care and surgical treatment after arriving with severe breathing difficulty and died despite the efforts of its medical teams.Tangila Islam Asha, 26, of Naugaon, told TOI that she and her husband, Mohammed Abdul Hakim Shabuj, 32, a contractual govt teacher in Bangladesh, arrived in Bengaluru on Sept 5 for treatment of his kidney ailment. Shabuj was admitted to ICU at Manipal Hospital on Old Airport Road the next day after developing severe chest pain and breathing difficulty.Asha said Shabuj underwent multiple procedures over the following days and his right leg was amputated on Sept 14 after it developed an infection. His condition subsequently deteriorated and he died around 1.30pm on Sept 18.“During his treatment, I paid a total of Rs 7.5 lakh in several instalments whenever they asked.After his death, I was trying to understand how I would take his body back to Bangladesh when the hospital asked me to pay Rs 35.79 lakh and said the body would not be released without payment,” Asha told TOI.She alleged that the hospital neither provided receipts for the Rs 7.5 lakh nor gave her a prior cost estimate or explanation for the outstanding amount. “I was completely helpless. After they withheld the body for eight days and retained my passport, I wrote to hospital management and also contacted Bangladesh High Commission for help. Finally, they handed over the body on Saturday after making the dues nil,” she said.Mohammed Moqtadir Hossain, Shabuj’s friend from West Bengal, who travelled to Bengaluru after learning of her situation, said local activists helped Asha recover her passport on Friday and complete formalities for taking the body home. “Apart from the Rs 7.5 lakh she had already paid, she paid nothing more,” he told TOI.When contacted, a Manipal Hospital office-bearer confirmed that the body was handed over on Saturday but declined to respond to Asha’s allegations. In a statement issued later, the hospital said Shabuj arrived with severe breathing difficulty, was found hypoxic and shifted to ICU, where he suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated twice before being put on ECMO and ventilator support.The hospital said surgeons performed a pulmonary thromboendarterectomy on Sept 9 after tests showed clot formation and blockages in several regions. “Despite best efforts from the critical care as well as the surgical team, the patient succumbed to his illnesses on 18th September 2026,” it said.’
Article Summary: Tangila Islam Asha, 26, received the body on Saturday after seeking help from Bangladesh High Commission. Manipal Hospital confirmed releasing the body but did not respond to her allegations. The hospital said the patient had undergone critical care and surgical treatment after arriving with severe breathing difficulty and died despite the efforts of its medical teams.

Article Title: ‘Damage control’ after EC row: Congress demands SIR rollback, CEC’s resignation
Article Text:
